case_title: Donor-derived fatal Strongyloides hyperinfection in a renal transplant recipient
disease_label_per_paper: Donor-derived fatal hyperinfection strongyloidiasis in a renal transplant recipient

source.title: Donor-derived fatal hyperinfection strongyloidiasis in renal transplant recipient

relevant_background: Deceased-donor renal transplant 2 months before presentation.
Induction and maintenance immunosuppression included basiliximab, mycophenolate mofetil, tacrolimus and corticosteroids.
At presentation he was receiving mycophenolate mofetil 750 mg twice daily, tacrolimus 6.5 mg twice daily and prednisolone 12.5 mg daily.
Valganciclovir and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis were being given.
Recipient pre-transplant Strongyloides serology was later confirmed negative; donor and the other kidney recipient were Strongyloides-seropositive.

chief_features: Subsequent acute respiratory failure, shock and paralytic ileus

risk_context.source_text: Renal transplant recipient 2 months post-transplant on tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil and prednisolone.
risk_context.source_text_value: Renal transplant recipient 2 months post-transplant on tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil and prednisolone.

risk_context.source_text: Basiliximab induction and ongoing triple immunosuppression with corticosteroids.
risk_context.source_text_value: Basiliximab induction and ongoing triple immunosuppression with corticosteroids.

risk_context.source_text: Maintenance prednisolone 12.5 mg daily after methylprednisolone induction.
risk_context.source_text_value: Maintenance prednisolone 12.5 mg daily after methylprednisolone induction.
Emesis and diarrhea were present at admission, followed by paralytic ileus that precluded enteral therapy.
The syndrome was initially treated as bacterial/viral/Pneumocystis pneumonia until BAL identified Strongyloides larvae.

observations.source_text: Oxygen saturation 100% in room air at admission.
Progressive shortness of breath over 3 days.
Initial white blood cell count 7.8 x 10^9/L.
Creatinine 2.19 mg/dL compared with 1.43 mg/dL 1 month earlier.
C-reactive protein reported as 127 mg/dL in the article table; encoded as 127 mg/L because this is the usual CRP reporting scale and magnitude for the clinical context.
observations.quality_note: Source unit ambiguity retained in source_text.

observations.source_text: Vomiting and diarrhea were present at admission but no ileus was yet documented.
No anti-Strongyloides therapy had been started at admission.
Creatinine had risen from 1.43 to 2.19 mg/dL in a renal transplant recipient.

course_observations.source_text: He developed severe acute respiratory failure with PaO2/FiO2 of 100.
He required endotracheal intubation and invasive mechanical ventilation.
Chest radiography showed bilateral interstitial infiltrates during respiratory failure.
He was intubated for severe acute respiratory failure.
He developed hemodynamic instability requiring noradrenaline.
Paralytic ileus was documented, precluding enteral therapy.
Shock, mechanical ventilation and paralytic ileus made oral treatment unreliable.
Bronchoalveolar lavage identified Strongyloides stercoralis larvae the day after ICU admission.
course_observations.leakage_note: Diagnostic confirmation evidence retained but should not be used when testing pre-confirmation ranking.

course_observations.source_text: Before ivermectin, the eosinophil count was 2200 cells/uL.
Subcutaneous ivermectin was started after Strongyloides larvae were found in BAL.
Multiple organ dysfunction progressed with renal failure requiring sustained low-efficiency daily dialysis.
He died of refractory multiorgan failure on the eighth day of admission.

values.source_text: Creatinine 1.43 mg/dL one month before admission.
No eosinophilia was reported in the initial hemogram.
Eosinophils rose to 2200 cells/uL before ivermectin.
CRP reported as 127 in the article table; encoded as mg/L with unit ambiguity noted.

imaging.findings: No significant ultrasound findings in the transplanted kidney evaluation.
Bilateral interstitial infiltrates during severe acute respiratory failure.
Purulent bronchial secretions were seen; bronchoalveolar lavage later identified Strongyloides larvae.

microbiology.note: Represents a documented bacterial coinfection signal rather than Strongyloides confirmation.
Supports donor-derived acquisition after the recipient had negative pre-transplant serology.

confirmatory_findings.finding: Strongyloides stercoralis larvae in bronchoalveolar lavage
Donor and contralateral kidney recipient Strongyloides seropositivity with recipient pre-transplant seronegativity

actual_treatment.details: Ciprofloxacin, ganciclovir and intravenous immunoglobulin were started initially while the syndrome was being evaluated.
Antibacterial therapy was changed to piperacillin-tazobactam and vancomycin when severe respiratory failure and shock developed.
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole was added for suspected Pneumocystis pneumonia before that diagnosis was excluded.
Mechanical ventilation, alveolar recruitment maneuvers, prone positioning and noradrenaline were used.
Because oral therapy was impossible in shock with paralytic ileus, subcutaneous ivermectin 200 micrograms/kg/day, 19 mg every 24 hours, was started.
Sustained low-efficiency daily dialysis was required for progressive renal failure.

outcome.cause_summary: Refractory multiple organ dysfunction after donor-derived Strongyloides hyperinfection with severe respiratory failure, shock, renal failure and later hepatic and hematologic failure.

quality_warnings: Diagnostic confirmation from BAL larvae, donor serology and recipient serology is retained but marked use_in_ranking=false for pre-confirmation tests.
The initial CRP unit in the source table appears inconsistent with common clinical reporting; the numeric value is encoded with unit ambiguity explicitly noted.
The case demonstrates absence of initial eosinophilia in a heavily immunosuppressed transplant recipient, with later eosinophilia before ivermectin.
